verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, a psalm, of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the leader of the singers: a song of David.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the superscription, and in the Hebrew text it counts as verse 1. That is why the KJV, which printed it as a heading, runs one verse behind from here to the end of the psalm. Do not play it as a title card; in the Temple liturgy someone spoke or sang it, and it tells the actors who is in the room. The 'choirmaster' is the leader of the Levitical musicians, and 'psalm' (mizmor) is a piece sung to stringed accompaniment. The preposition on 'David' is the interesting word. It can mean 'by David', 'for David' or 'about David', and the Hebrew commentators split: Radak and Metzudat David take it as a prayer said on David's behalf when he went out to war, and Ibn Ezra reads it as another poet writing for David. The KJV's 'A Psalm of David' flattens that choice into authorship.

philological_notes.note: 'For the leader/choirmaster', a participle from a root that means to be pre-eminent or to excel. The old versions guessed 'to the chief musician'; the exact office is uncertain.
The ל can mean 'by', 'for' or 'concerning'. The commentators argue over it, and the translation keeps it open.

verses.translation_literal: May YHWH answer you in the day of distress; may the name of the God of Jacob set you on high.
verses.translation_dramatic: May the LORD answer you on the day the walls close in. May the name of the God of Jacob lift you out of reach, high above everything that threatens you.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice is plural and spoken to one man: the congregation addresses the king (the psalm does not name him, but the superscription sends us to David) as he leaves for war. Play it as a send-off, tight and intimate, like a blessing given at a gate. 'Day of distress' is a stock phrase for the day of battle; tzarah comes from a root meaning 'narrow', so it is the day you are in a tight place. The verb 'set on high' (sagav) is the language of the fortress: it means to place someone out of an attacker's reach, which gives us the noun misgav, 'stronghold'. The KJV's 'defend' is acceptable but it loses the height. The KJV also says 'hear' for 'answer': in Hebrew to 'answer' is to act in response, not merely to listen. 'The name of the God of Jacob' is chosen on purpose. Jacob is the patriarch who knew flight, exile and fear, and the commentators connect the title to a God who answered him in his own distress (Rashi, Radak, Ibn Ezra). In the ancient world a deity's name was a presence and a power, not a label, so 'the name' stands for God acting.

philological_notes.note: 'May he answer you'. In the Psalms, 'to answer' means to respond with help, not only to hear, so 'hear' in the KJV is too weak.
From a root meaning 'to be high, inaccessible'. The piel means to put someone beyond reach; it is the verb of a fortress (misgav). Radak compares help to a strong tower.

'The name of the God of Jacob'. The name stands for God's power and presence. Meiri says the name and the God are one; the commentators relate 'Jacob' either to the patriarch's troubles or to all Israel.

verses.translation_literal: May he send your help from the holy place, and from Zion may he support you.
verses.translation_dramatic: May he send you help from the holy place. From Zion, from the hill where his house stands, may he hold you up.
verses.directors_commentary: Now the blessing has a direction. The speakers stand at the sanctuary and look outward toward the army; help is sent from the place where God's presence is, and 'from Zion' answers 'from the holy place' in the usual parallel pair. Radak and Meiri tie this to the ark, which in earlier days went out to war and now stays in Zion, so Zion is where the king's help is stored. Metzudat David says the two lines simply double the same thought. The KJV's 'sanctuary' and 'out of Zion' are fine; the gap is 'strengthen', for the verb sa'ad means to prop up, to support from underneath, a picture of a man who is held by his arms rather than made stronger. For modern actors: the king is going to the field, and the people stay behind in the holy place; everything they can do for him is to ask.

philological_notes.note: 'May he support you', from a root meaning to prop up or sustain. The nominal form is 'support', as Metzudat Zion says, and it is closer to bracing than to strengthening.
'From the holy place'. Rashi takes it as God's holy dwelling; Radak and Metzudat David as the house where the ark was. Meiri also allows heaven.

verses.translation_literal: May he remember all your offerings, and your burnt offering may he make fat. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: May he remember every gift you have laid before him, and may the fire take your burnt offering, rich and rising, and he find it good. Selah. Hold the silence.
verses.directors_commentary: The congregation names two kinds of sacrifice. The minchah is a gift offering, usually of grain; the olah, 'that which goes up', is the burnt offering consumed whole on the altar. The commentators say that before a campaign the king's offerings were brought, and the people now ask God to 'remember' them. In Hebrew, to remember is not only to recall but to act on what is recalled, so the request is that the earlier gifts count in the king's favour. The hard word is yedashsheneh. The KJV's 'accept' is a guess at the sense; the verb is built on deshen, which means both 'fat, richness' and 'the ashes of the altar'. So the wish is that God make the sacrifice rich, that it be consumed and accepted. Rashi reads it as 'accept it favourably, like a fat burnt offering'; Ibn Ezra, as 'may the altar fire burn it into ash'. YLT's 'reduce to ashes' captures one half. 'Selah' is a mark of a pause or musical interlude; do not try to say what it means. Let the actors stop.

philological_notes.note: From deshen, 'fat; ashes of the altar'. The piel means to make fat/rich, so to treat the offering as acceptable, or to reduce it to ashes. The -eh ending is irregular; Radak and Meiri compare 'we'eqra'eh' in 1 Sam 28:15.
'May he remember'. In biblical Hebrew the verb carries the action that follows memory; Ibn Ezra links it to the trumpet-law of Numbers 10:9 ('you will be remembered before the LORD').
A mark of uncertain meaning, probably a pause or musical interlude. Not translated.

verses.translation_literal: May he give you according to your heart, and all your counsel may he fill.
verses.translation_dramatic: May he give you what your heart has set out to find, and bring every plan you have laid to its full measure.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Heart' in Hebrew is the seat of thought and will, not of sentiment, so 'according to your heart' means your intention and your design. The pairing with 'counsel' (etzah) confirms it: this is the battle plan, and the wish is that it works. Radak points to Proverbs 24:6, 'with strategy you wage war'. The KJV's 'fulfil' for 'fill' is fair, but 'fill' is the Hebrew picture: a plan is a vessel, and God fills it. The KJV's 'thine own heart' adds 'own', which the Hebrew does not say. Radak records a midrash that only David could be addressed this way, since for an ordinary person the heart might desire something wrong; to others one says 'fulfil your requests' instead. That is a later comment on the text, not part of the verse, but it helps an actor see the confidence of the speakers.

philological_notes.note: 'Your counsel, your plan'. A military plan in this setting; Radak cites Proverbs 24:6 and 2 Kings 18:20.
'May he fill', the same verb as in v. 6b, which makes a frame: the blessing of v. 5 returns as 'fill all your requests'.

verses.translation_literal: We will shout for joy at your salvation, and in the name of our God we will raise a banner. May YHWH fill all your requests.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then we will sing out for joy at the victory you win. In the name of our God we will lift our banners high, and may the LORD fill all that you have asked.
verses.directors_commentary: The speakers move from 'may he' to 'we will', from asking to promising. Verbs of joy and banner-raising come in the future: the army will celebrate when the king is saved, and march under the name. The word for 'shout for joy' (ranan) is a ringing cry, not a quiet gladness. The word 'banner' (degel) is a military standard, a rallying flag of a tribal division, so 'in the name of our God we raise the banner' means that the banner will carry a god's name, a direct contrast with the royal and divine standards of the neighbours. Rashi connects the verb to the gathering of the army (Ps 60:14, KJV 60:12). Where the KJV has 'we will rejoice', the Hebrew keeps the sound of a shout. Note also that 'salvation' (yeshuah) here is the king's deliverance, which in the Bible means rescue in battle, not a spiritual state. The last clause is a wish again, and it closes the frame begun in v. 5.

philological_notes.note: 'We will shout for joy'; the cohortative has a ring-cry sense, the shout of a crowd.
'We will raise a banner'. From degel, a standard. Rashi explains it as 'we gather and become a host' by comparison with Ps 60:14 (KJV 60:12); Radak as 'we lift our banner and our standard'.
'Your requests, what you have asked'. The KJV's 'petitions' is correct but formal.

verses.translation_literal: Now I know that YHWH has saved his anointed; he will answer him from his holy heavens, with the mighty deeds of the salvation of his right hand.
verses.translation_dramatic: Now I know it. The LORD has saved his anointed. He answers him from the heavens of his holiness, with the strength of a right hand that saves.
verses.directors_commentary: A turn: the plural 'we' falls silent and one voice says 'I know'. Who is speaking is a real question. Ibn Ezra takes it as the psalmist speaking by the Holy Spirit; Radak and Meiri as each Israelite; Malbim as the leader of the singers answering the choir. Whoever it is, the grammar changes: the wishes of vv. 2-6 become a statement, and 'has saved' is a perfect tense, a completed act that the speaker states with certainty. Perhaps news has arrived. 'His anointed' (meshicho) is the king, set apart by anointing with oil; the KJV leaves it 'anointed', and BBE's 'king' interprets. For the king to be called God's own anointed is the heart of royal theology: Radak says the people declare, against the enemies who said there is no salvation for him in God (Ps 3:3), that he is indeed chosen. 'From his holy heavens' is plural in Hebrew (shamei), a plural of form that YLT reproduces ('holy heavens'), where KJV and ASV have the singular 'heaven'. 'Right hand' is the hand of strength and action; the phrase 'mighty deeds of the salvation of his right hand' piles up nouns in a way the KJV's 'saving strength' smooths. In an actor's mouth, this is the sound of relief arriving.

philological_notes.note: 'His anointed'. A king set apart by oil. Radak and Metzudat David read it as David; Ibn Ezra allows David or his descendant the Messiah.
'From the heavens of his holiness'. The word for heaven is a plural of form, as in YLT's 'holy heavens'; it contrasts with the earthly 'holy place' of v. 3.
'He has saved', the perfect: a completed act in the speaker's certainty, so the KJV 'saveth' (a present) is less exact.

verses.translation_literal: These [trust] in chariotry, and these in horses, and we, in the name of YHWH our God, we make mention.
verses.translation_dramatic: Some come with chariots. Some come with horses. But we, we call up the name of the LORD our God.
verses.directors_commentary: The best-known verse of the psalm is also the most compressed. The Hebrew has no verb for the first two clauses: 'these in chariotry, and these in horses'. KJV and ASV supply 'trust'; YLT supplies nothing, and the Webster brackets it. Chariots and horses are the strike force of the Bronze and Iron Age: the chariot is the armoured, expensive weapon of kings, and Israel's hill-country troops had none to match. Radak cites Isaiah 31:1, 'they trust in chariots because they are many'. The last verb nazkir is the puzzle. It is the causative of 'to remember', so it means 'we cause [the name] to be remembered', that is, we call on it, pronounce it, bring it to mind. KJV's 'remember' loses the causative; ASV's 'make mention of' is closer. Rashi hears the cultic sense, as with incense and offering (Lev 2:2, Isa 66:3), so naming God is itself a form of worship and appeal. Do not play the verse as smug. It is the voice of an outnumbered army.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of 'to remember': 'to cause to be remembered, to invoke, to call to mind', with the name as object. Rashi relates it to the cultic hiphil in Isaiah 66:3 and Leviticus 2:2.
'In the chariotry'. A collective singular: not one chariot but the force. The preposition marks the thing relied on.

verses.translation_literal: They, they bowed down and fell; and we, we rose and were set upright.
verses.translation_dramatic: They sank to their knees, and they fell. And we got up. We stood, and we are standing still.
verses.directors_commentary: The two halves are a mirror. 'They' and 'we' are both stated outright, though Hebrew verbs already carry the person, so the pronouns are a stress: they, and we. The enemy bends the knee and drops; Israel rises. The KJV's 'brought down' and 'risen' are right, but 'bowed down' is the actual verb: kara' is to sink on the knees, as a man or an animal does when it collapses. Ibn Ezra notices that the two verbs split the enemy into two groups, kneeling charioteers and fallen riders. The last verb (vanit'odad) is rare: a reflexive of a root meaning 'to be upright / to be held up', related to the word for God who 'lifts up the humble' (Ps 147:6, Rashi). KJV 'stand upright' is the picture. Perfect tenses throughout: the speakers narrate it as already done.

philological_notes.note: A rare reflexive, 'and we were set upright / we stood firm'. Rashi and Metzudat Zion tie it to 'me'oded anavim' (Ps 147:6), 'who holds up the humble'.
'They sank to their knees'. The verb is a collapse, not an act of reverence.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, save! May the King answer us in the day of our calling.
verses.translation_dramatic: O LORD, save! Let the King answer us on the day we call.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm ends as a battle cry, a short prayer the army can shout. The Hebrew can be divided two ways. YLT reads 'O Jehovah, save the king', joining 'the king' to the verb. KJV, ASV and BBE follow the accent, which breaks after 'save', but their rendering of 'the king' leaves open who answers: the KJV's lowercase 'let the king hear us' can be the human king or God. Ibn Ezra, who prefers the reading that 'the King is the LORD', Radak and Meiri take 'the King' as God himself, the heavenly king, the answerer of the next clause: 'LORD, save! May the King answer us.' Ibn Ezra rejects joining 'the king' to 'save' because of the atnach after 'save'. Malbim instead has King David answering, saying 'LORD, save'. The accent-based reading also fits the frame of the psalm, which began with 'May YHWH answer you' and ends with 'the King answer us', and the verb 'answer' is used at the start, in the middle (v. 7) and the end. Radak says the cry was literally shouted in battle. 'Calling' (qare'enu) closes with the same word that Hebrew uses for a battle shout and for prayer. Reading it as YLT does makes the army pray for its human king, which is also possible, so keep both open for the actor: the voice that shouts is the army, and the King may be either.

philological_notes.note: 'The King'. Either God (Ibn Ezra as his preferred reading, Radak, Meiri) or the human king (YLT, and Malbim, who has King David answering). The accent after 'hoshiah' favours a break before it.
An imperative with the -ah ending: 'save!'. It is the cry that gave the word 'hosanna'.
